exam: What bedside steps differentiate cervical ectropion from infectious cervicitis? — Look for red, smooth area without purulent discharge; obtain wet mount and consider NAAT for chlamydia.

A 28‑year‑old pregnant woman reports post‑coital spotting. Speculum shows a red area around the os. What is your next management? — Reassure, document ectropion, advise gentle intercourse; no treatment unless bleeding is heavy.
How does high estrogen physiologically cause ectropion? — Estrogen stimulates columnar cell proliferation and reduces squamous maturation, allowing columnar epithelium to evert.
When is cryotherapy indicated for cervical ectropion? — When the ectropion is symptomatic, bleeds repeatedly, or persists despite medical therapy and colposcopy rules out neoplasia.
A woman on combined oral contraceptives presents with mucopurulent discharge and ectropion. Which investigation is essential? — Perform a NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis; treat if positive.
Why might a VIA test be falsely negative in a patient with ectropion? — The red columnar surface can obscure acetowhite changes, reducing test sensitivity.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral to a gynaecologic oncology unit? — Persistent ulceration or friable tissue with atypical cells on colposcopic biopsy.
Explain why topical estrogen is preferred over systemic estrogen for post‑menopausal ectropion. — Local therapy restores squamous epithelium with minimal systemic exposure and lower thrombotic risk.
ai.title: Cervical Ectropion
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Cervical ectropion is the outward migration of columnar endocervical epithelium onto the ectocervical surface, appearing as a red, vascular area around the os. It is usually benign but can cause symptoms and mimic pathology, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Red, velvety area around the external os
Often seen in reproductive‑age women, pregnant women, and oral contraceptive users
sections.p: When the glandular columnar epithelium of the endocervix extends onto the squamous ectocervix, the exposed area looks red and friable. Diagnosis is visual, using a speculum and adequate lighting; no biopsy is needed unless suspicious lesions coexist.

b: Mild: <25% of the os circumference
Moderate: 25‑50% involvement
Severe: >50% involvement or associated ulceration
sections.p: There is no formal staging system; clinicians grade severity by the proportion of the os involved:

b: High estrogen states – pregnancy, oral contraceptives, hormone replacement
Physiological puberty
Chronic irritation – frequent douching, herbal pessaries
Infections – HIV, chronic cervicitis, chlamydia
Rare: cervical neoplasia causing eversion
sections.p: Ectropion results from hormonal stimulation or local irritation that promotes columnar cell migration.

b: Post‑coital bleeding
Mucopurulent discharge
Dyspareunia
Vaginal itching from secondary infection
sections.p: Many women are asymptomatic; when symptoms occur they relate to the exposed columnar epithelium.
Focus on confirming ectropion and excluding co‑existing pathology.

t.b: Is the red area consistent with ectropion or suspicious for lesion? → Visual confirmation; if suspicious, proceed to colposcopy/biopsy.
Is the cervical environment acidic (pH < 4.5) or alkaline? → Ectropion often raises pH; an alkaline pH suggests bacterial vaginosis or STI.
Are there clue cells, trichomonads, or yeast? → Guides treatment of secondary infection.
Is the patient HIV positive? → HIV increases chronic cervicitis and may worsen ectropion.
Is there any acetowhite change, atypia, or lesion beyond ectropion? → Determines need for biopsy.

b: Persistent ulceration or friable tissue
Unexplained weight loss or systemic symptoms
Positive VIA/VILI suggesting neoplasia
Severe, uncontrolled bleeding
sections.p: Although usually benign, certain features demand urgent evaluation.

b: Reassure asymptomatic women; no intervention needed.
Topical estrogen cream (low‑dose) for post‑menopausal atrophy – promotes squamous maturation.
Avoid irritants – discontinue douching, harsh soaps, and untested herbal pessaries.
Cryotherapy or electrocautery only if lesion persists, bleeds heavily, or suspicion of neoplasia.
sections.p: Treat the cause, relieve symptoms, and monitor for change.

b: Educate on safe sexual practices and genital hygiene.
Encourage regular Pap smears (or VIA in low‑resource settings).
Consider switching to non‑estrogenic contraception if symptoms are estrogen‑driven.
sections.p: Schedule review after 6‑12 weeks if treatment was given; otherwise annual cervical screening suffices.

b: Cervicitis (infective inflammation)
Cervical polyps (smooth, pedunculated growth)
Early invasive carcinoma (irregular, ulcerated, acetowhite on colposcopy)
HPV‑related condyloma (wart‑like lesions)
sections.p: Conditions that also present with red cervical changes.

b: Normal pH does not exclude ectropion; columnar cells may still be present.
Negative wet mount does not rule out chlamydia – need NAAT if available.
Absence of visible lesion on speculum does not exclude early neoplasia; VIA may miss subtle changes.

whenToSeekHelp: Visible ulcer or necrotic tissue on the cervix
Positive HIV test with new cervical symptoms
